title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Stars Went Out
moral: The bravest thing is not to act without fear, but to act in spite of it.

pages.content: The first sign that something was wrong was the absence of the fireflies. They had lit the meadow above the old ridge every night since {{NAME}} could remember, their slow, patient blinking as reliable as breathing. Tonight the meadow was dark. All of it. Even the moon looked thinner, as if something was drawing its light away slowly, the way cold draws heat from a room. {{NAME}} arrived at the ridge to find the animals already gathered, anxious and clustered: a parliament of owls perched in absolute silence, a badger named Sable standing with her thick paws pressed together, a young fox cub named Gorse who kept looking up at the sky with enormous worried eyes. At the centre of the gathered animals stood Celestine, a unicorn whose coat carried the whole night sky within it, galaxies swirling slowly across her flank. Even her light was dimmer than {{NAME}} had ever seen it. 'The Luminance is fading,' Celestine said. Her voice was very calm, which somehow made it worse.

pages.content: Celestine explained with a stillness that {{NAME}} found more frightening than panic. The Luminance was the living light that fed the stars and the fireflies and every bioluminescent creature from the deep-sea lanternfish to the smallest glow-worm under a garden stone. Something had tangled it, a knot forming in the great invisible thread of light that connected all luminous things. She could feel the knot's location: at the very peak of the Cloudspire, four hours' flight away. Four hours by wing. 'I cannot fly,' Sable the badger said flatly. 'My wings are decorative.' She extended two very small and completely impractical wings from her back and folded them again with dignity. Gorse the fox cub looked at {{NAME}}, then at his cape. 'You can,' said the cub. {{NAME}} felt a cold knot of his own forming in his chest. He had never flown to the Cloudspire. He had never flown at night. He had never done anything the Luminance needed him to do. 'I'll need a guide,' he said. Celestine stepped forward and touched her horn to his cape, and the fabric shimmered and steadied, as if it had been given a direction.

pages.content: Flying at night above a dark world with no stars felt like swimming in ink. {{NAME}} held the direction Celestine had pressed into his cape like a compass bearing, following the faint warmth it gave off whenever he turned toward the Cloudspire. The wind at this height was cold and serious. Below him the hills were dark lumps, the rivers thin threads without their usual glimmer. He was not alone. Gorse ran below on the ground, tracking by smell, calling up direction corrections that {{NAME}} could just hear if he dropped low enough, and Sable had produced, from somewhere practical, a lantern of captured fireflies that she held at the ridge below as a home-bearing. Even the parliament of owls tracked silently above him, their great wings carrying them without effort, a slow dark constellation. When the Cloudspire appeared through the night haze, it was unmistakeable: a single column of rock driving upward through the clouds like a finger pointing at the empty sky. At its peak, visible even from here, was a knot of light, pulsing desperately, like a trapped heartbeat.

pages.content: The knot at the Cloudspire's peak was not a thing with teeth or claws. It was not a villain or a monster. It was simply a tangle, a place where the threads of light had knotted around a jutting shard of rock, pulled tighter by their own weight over years and years, until now the flow had almost stopped. {{NAME}} landed on the spire's narrow peak and looked at it. His hands shook. The wind was savage up here. But the knot was actually not so different from the ones he untangled in his bicycle chain, or the shoelace knots that IRON-OWL had once pointed out. He took one breath. He began to work. He could not see the threads of light with his eyes. He could feel them with his fingertips, warm and humming, vibrating with urgency. Loop by loop, he worked in the dark. It took a long time. His fingers ached. And then the knot released, and the light moved through it, and the effect was immediate and catastrophic and wonderful: every star in the sky ignited at once, blazing into existence like a thousand simultaneous dawns, and the world below shook with the sound of every firefly, every glow-worm, every bioluminescent creature on earth blazing back to life together.

pages.content: When {{NAME}} returned to the ridge meadow, Celestine was blazing. Her coat was alive with galaxies in full colour, swirling and brilliant, the way they must have been before the Luminance had faded. The fireflies were back, hundreds of them, moving through the grass in their slow, patient patterns. Sable had put out her lantern and was watching the fireflies with an expression of pure relief that she would probably deny if anyone mentioned it. Gorse sat at {{NAME}}'s feet and pressed his small warm head against {{NAME}}'s shin. The owls had returned to their oak and resumed whatever silent parliament business owls do at three in the morning. Celestine lowered her blazing horn to {{NAME}}'s shoulder, and he felt warmth run all the way down to his cold and aching fingertips. 'Go home,' she said gently. 'Sleep.' He was too tired to fly and walked home through the fields instead, the fireflies keeping pace with him through the long grass all the way to his gate, as if making sure he arrived safely. He fell asleep the moment his head found the pillow. He dreamed of light. He wondered, just at the edge of dreams, what else in the world was quietly waiting to be untangled.
